About | The Core Centennial

# 100 Years of the Core

Columbia College celebrates a century of dialogue and debate through a year of festivities and conversation.

## The Core Curriculum

Since 1919, the Core Curriculum has been the centerpiece of the undergraduate intellectual experience at Columbia College. 

The Core Curriculum consists of five courses that all students at the College take, four of them on important books and works of art and music in the Western tradition, and one on scientific inquiry and discovery. In addition to these courses, students have a two-course Global Core requirement and take a course in University Writing (formerly Logic & Rhetoric). The Core is meant to prompt students to grapple with fundamental questions of human existence and to think deeply about how the contemporary world has been shaped by the past, while also honing students’ skills of analysis, clear and cogent argumentation, and persuasive exposition.

The content and organization of the Core Curriculum are guided by the view that the ultimate ends of a liberal education necessarily reflect a vision of the ultimate ends of a human life. The conversations across disciplines and specializations that sustain the Core Curriculum as a non-disciplinary requirement for all students also give it its vitality and force. They represent an exercise in the complex arts of consensus-building, compromise, and honest debate—liberal habits of mind that we hold as fundamental to the education we aim to provide and to the intellectual communities we wish to foster.

## History of the Core

1919 

### A Course About Peace 

“Introduction to Contemporary Civilization in the West” is introduced following the end of World War I with a civic focus. The class meets five days a week for an hour each day.

1920 

### Literature Humanities is envisioned 

The General Honors course is introduced; it is built around “great books”, read in translation and discussed in small groups. This was the predecessor to Humanities B, which eventually became Literature Humanities.

1937 

### Humanities expands to include art and music 

Humanities A and Humanities B are introduced; Humanities A focused on classic texts of literature and philosophy and Humanities B focused on visual arts and music.

1941 

### Art and Music Humanities are born 

Humanities B formally splits into two, with Humanities B1 becoming “Music Humanities” and Humanities B2 evolving into “Art Humanities.” Each class meets three times a week, with one lecture and two smaller discussion seminars.

1947 

### The first Oriental Studies program in the nation 

Professor Theodore de Bary CC’41 introduces the first “Oriental Studies” program in the country, with the course “Oriental Humanities” (modeled on Lit Hum). In 1950, “Oriental Civilization” (modeled on CC) is introduced.

1968 

### “Redbooks” and “Revolutions” 

The CC syllabus substitutes source books with entire texts, thus eliminating the compiled source books used in the class. The spring semester focused on “Revolutions”, addressing the student protests at Columbia and around the nation.

1985 

### A Female Author Joins Lit Hum 

Two years after women are admitted to Columbia College, Jane Austen is the first woman author included on the Literature Humanities course with the addition of "Pride and Prejudice.”

1990 

### Non-Western Cultures Become Required 

An “Extended Core” requirement is introduced whereby students must take courses on cultures not covered in Lit Hum and CC, choosing from a list of electives in Asian, African, Latin American or Native American civilization.

2004 

### Science Becomes the Fifth Shared Course 

“Frontiers of Science” is introduced in order to instill “scientific habits of mind” and to encourage students to think about the world around them and the ways in which science can help us answer questions about nature and ourselves.

2019 

### A Century of Core Conversations 

Columbia College celebrates a century of what began as an intellectual experiment, meant to address “the insistent problems of our time.” 

## Support the Core

For 10 decades, the Core Curriculum has cultivated our students’ curiosity and thirst for deep inquiry. Support the next century of this distinctive experience by supporting us in our Centennial year and beyond.
